title: Production incident response
description: A drill for the engineer holding the pager: from the first alert to a closed incident.

states.name: Page received
states.description: A monitor fired and your phone is buzzing. Nobody else has picked this up yet, and the escalation timer is running.
states.annotation: Acknowledge within five minutes, even if you have no idea what is wrong yet.

states.name: Acknowledge the page
states.description: You have claimed the incident. The escalation timer stops and the rest of the team can see who is driving.

states.name: Assess the impact
states.description: You are reading the dashboards and the recent deploy log, deciding whether real users are affected right now or whether a threshold was simply crossed.

states.name: Watch and wait
states.description: Nothing is clearly broken. You are watching the error rate and latency graphs for fifteen minutes before deciding anything.
states.annotation: Set a timer. Watching forever is how a small incident becomes a long one.

states.name: Declare an incident
states.description: You have confirmed user impact and said so out loud in the incident channel. From here the work is coordinated rather than solo.

states.name: Gather responders
states.description: You are pulling in the people who own the failing system and naming who does what, so two engineers do not fix the same thing twice.

states.name: Escalate
states.description: Nobody in the room can move the incident forward. You are paging a senior engineer or the service owner and saying plainly what you have tried.

states.name: Mitigate
states.description: You are stopping the bleeding: shifting traffic, disabling the new feature flag, or scaling the starved component.
states.annotation: Mitigation comes before diagnosis. Understanding why can wait until users are served again.

states.name: Roll back the deploy
states.description: The mitigation did not hold, and the suspect change is recent. You are putting the previous known-good build back in place.

states.name: Monitor recovery
states.description: Traffic is flowing again and the graphs are pointing the right way. You are watching long enough to be sure it holds.

states.name: Write the postmortem
states.description: The incident is over. You are recording the timeline, the contributing causes and the follow-up work while the details are fresh.
states.annotation: Blameless means naming the system that let this happen, not the person who pressed the button.

states.name: Close as alert noise
states.description: No user was ever affected and the alert fired on a threshold that is too tight. You are closing the incident and filing a ticket to fix the alert.

states.name: Hand over to the next shift
states.description: The incident is still open but your shift is done. You are writing a handover note covering what is known, what was tried and what the next person should do first.

transitions.label: Acknowledge the page
transitions.description: Claim the incident so everyone knows who is driving.

transitions.label: This alert is a known false positive
A senior engineer takes over the fix
The previous build is live again
The symptoms came back
transitions.description: Recovery was partial: treat it as a live incident again.
